reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
clinicalPearls: Peliosis hepatis is a rare vascular disorder in which the liver contains multiple blood-filled cystic spaces due to dilatation of the hepatic sinusoids.

It is classically drug- or toxin-associated, with anabolic androgenic steroids, oestrogens and oral contraceptives, corticosteroids, tamoxifen and thiopurines such as azathioprine among the recognised culprits.
It also complicates chronic wasting states such as advanced malignancy, tuberculosis and malnutrition, as well as solid-organ transplantation.
Bacillary peliosis caused by Bartonella species in immunocompromised hosts is an important infective mimic to consider but is a separate entity.
Most cases are asymptomatic and found incidentally; when symptomatic there may be hepatomegaly, cholestatic or mixed enzyme derangement and portal hypertension.
The feared complication is spontaneous rupture of a peliotic cavity causing life-threatening intraperitoneal haemorrhage and haemodynamic collapse.
Imaging is non-specific and easily confused with metastases, abscess or haemangioma, and percutaneous biopsy carries a significant bleeding risk.
Withdrawal of the offending agent often leads to regression, and management is otherwise supportive, with embolisation or resection reserved for bleeding.
reference.pathophysiology: Peliosis hepatis results from injury to the hepatic sinusoidal endothelium and the reticulin framework that supports the hepatocyte plates. Loss of this support allows the sinusoids to dilate into blood-filled lacunar spaces distributed randomly throughout the parenchyma. Two histological patterns are described: a parenchymal type in which the cavities lack an endothelial lining and communicate with disrupted hepatocytes, and a phlebectatic type in which endothelium-lined spaces are centred on dilated central veins. Hormonal, cytotoxic and immunosuppressive agents are thought to weaken the sinusoidal wall and impair outflow, while chronic infection or wasting may act through endothelial injury and altered hepatic blood flow. Because the cavities are thin-walled and engorged they are prone to rupture, and extensive involvement can compress adjacent parenchyma and impair hepatic function.
additionalDifferentials: Multifocal simple cysts or biliary hamartomas
Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome or Budd-Chiari syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Multiphase contrast-enhanced CT of the liver
Doppler ultrasound of the hepatic vasculature
Careful, often transjugular, liver biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain
Full liver function panel and coagulation profile
Detailed drug and medication history including performance-enhancing agents
Screen for underlying malignancy or chronic infection
redFlags: Sudden severe abdominal pain with hypotension suggesting cavity rupture and haemoperitoneum
Progressive hepatic dysfunction or synthetic failure
New portal hypertension with variceal bleeding
reference.prognosis: Drug-associated disease frequently regresses once the causative agent is stopped, but spontaneous rupture or extensive parenchymal involvement carries a high mortality and may precipitate hepatic failure.
pitfalls: Performing a routine percutaneous biopsy of a vascular lesion and provoking major haemorrhage.
Misdiagnosing the lesions as metastatic malignancy and subjecting the patient to unnecessary treatment.
Failing to take a thorough medication and anabolic-steroid history.
Overlooking the diagnosis as a cause of unexplained intra-abdominal haemorrhage.
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
management: Withdraw the causative drug or toxin such as anabolic androgenic steroids, oestrogens, tamoxifen, corticosteroids or thiopurines like azathioprine, as disease often regresses once the agent is stopped

Treat the underlying wasting or infective condition such as tuberculosis, malignancy or malnutrition, and manage bacillary peliosis from Bartonella in the immunocompromised with appropriate antimicrobials

Manage spontaneous intraperitoneal haemorrhage as an emergency with resuscitation, transfusion and correction of coagulopathy, achieving haemostasis by transarterial embolisation or surgery including hepatic resection
Monitor lesions with serial cross-sectional imaging to confirm regression after removal of the precipitant
Support hepatic dysfunction and portal hypertension where present
Refer to hepatology and interventional radiology, particularly when the diagnosis is uncertain or rupture is a risk
